title: Mold Spread
statement: A pantry shelf is a grid of equal-length rows: 'F' is fresh bread, 'S' is spoiled bread and '.' is empty space. Every minute, each fresh loaf that shares an edge (up, down, left or right) with a spoiled loaf becomes spoiled. Return the number of minutes until no fresh bread remains, 0 if there is no fresh bread at the start, or -1 if some fresh loaf can never spoil.
constraints: 1 <= grid[i].length <= 100, all rows have equal length

examples.explanation: Mold reaches the bottom-right loaf after 4 minutes.
The loaf in the bottom-left corner touches nothing, so it never spoils.

hints.content: Simulating minute by minute works but rescans the whole shelf each minute.
A loaf spoils at the minute equal to its distance (in edge steps through bread) from the nearest initially spoiled loaf.
Breadth-first search computes shortest distances, and it can start from many sources at once.
Put every initially spoiled loaf in the first layer. Each layer spoils its fresh neighbors and forms the next layer.
Count fresh loaves up front and decrement as they spoil. The number of layers that spoiled something is the answer; leftover fresh bread means -1.

testCases.explanation: Mold reaches the bottom-right loaf after 4 minutes.
The loaf in the bottom-left corner touches nothing, so it never spoils.
Fresh bread with no mold can never spoil.
Mold spreads from both ends and meets in the middle after 2 minutes.
From the corner the farthest loaf is 5 steps away.
Diagonal neighbors do not count, so the fresh corners never spoil.
Every fresh loaf touches mold: 1 minute.

solutions.title: Simulate whole-shelf minutes
solutions.intuition: Apply the rule exactly as stated, one minute at a time.
solutions.approach: Each minute, build a new grid where a fresh loaf next to spoiled bread becomes spoiled. Stop when no fresh bread remains (return the minute) or when a minute changes nothing (return -1).
solutions.pseudocode:
for minute = 0..: if no F: return minute
  next = grid with each F adjacent to S turned to S
  if next == grid: return -1; grid = next
commonMistakes: Updating the grid in place, which lets mold spread several cells in a single minute.
Looping forever when some fresh bread is unreachable.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A direct simulation with a copied grid each minute respects the 'everything spoils simultaneously' rule. It rescans the full grid every minute, so it's quadratic in the number of cells.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Minute 1 spoils (0,1) and (1,0); minute 2 spoils (0,2) and (1,1).

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Minute 3 spoils (2,1); minute 4 spoils (2,2). No fresh bread remains, so return 4.

solutions.title: Multi-source breadth-first search
solutions.intuition: Spoiling time is the shortest distance from any initial mold, which a BFS seeded with all molds computes directly.
solutions.approach: Queue every 'S' cell and count every 'F'. While the queue and fresh count are non-zero, process one layer: spoil each fresh neighbor, decrement the fresh count, enqueue it. Count layers. Return -1 if fresh bread remains.
solutions.pseudocode:
queue = all S; fresh = count F; minutes = 0
while queue and fresh: next = []; for cell in queue: for neighbor F: mark S; fresh--; next.push
  queue = next; minutes++
return fresh ? -1 : minutes
commonMistakes: Running a separate BFS from each spoiled loaf and taking minimums, which repeats work.
Counting the final empty layer as an extra minute; stop as soon as fresh reaches zero.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Each loaf spoils at its shortest distance from any initial mold, so I run one BFS with every spoiled loaf as a source. Each layer is one minute. I mark cells when I enqueue them so nothing is processed twice, and a fresh counter tells me when to stop and whether anything stayed unreachable. Linear in the number of cells.
